## Step 14 — Rename-Safe Parts, Meshes, and Entities ✅

Per direct request: "I want to make it trivial to rename parts, meshes or entities without it breaking relations." Today's model has no separate display name anywhere -- a part's `"id"` is the only handle other parts' `attachTo.part` and animation clips' `"parts"`/`"origins"` maps point at, a mesh's `"id"` is the only handle every referencing part's `"mesh"` field points at, and an entity's `"id"` is the only handle `render_template` points at. `launcher.py`'s own pre-existing `_rename_asset()` docstring already admitted the hazard plainly: "does not scan other entities/areas for references to the old id."

Two structural fixes were possible: cascade a rename across every known reference type (fragile forever -- a future reference type not taught to the renamer reintroduces this exact bug class), or give every part/mesh/entity a permanent internal id that references are keyed on, with a separate, freely-editable display name that renaming actually touches. **User chose the latter, confirmed via `AskUserQuestion` before implementing** (a genuine architecture fork). Also confirmed: the id should stay a **readable slug frozen at creation**, not become an opaque token -- ids are already readable strings (`mesh-l_wing`, `shaft`), every combo/header in this tool displays them as the human-facing string today, and freezing a slug costs nothing extra while preserving grep/debuggability.

1. **Real bug found and fixed as a prerequisite, confirmed by inspection, not theorized**: `tools/convert_mesh.py`'s `convert()` derived both `"id"` and `"name"` from `in_path.stem` (the *source* `.glb`'s filename) instead of `output_path` (what the caller actually asked the output to be named) -- `entity_builder.py`'s "Convert Mesh"/"Split Multi-Mesh GLB" buttons let the user type an independent output id, but that choice was silently ignored for the JSON's own `id`/`name` fields. This is the exact, confirmed cause of a real, live duplicate-id collision already in the asset tree: `frontend/assets/data/mesh/mesh-bird.json` and `mesh-body.json` were byte-identical, both converted from a source file literally named `body.glb` at different times into two different output filenames, but both stamped `"id": "mesh-body"`. Fixed by deriving from `Path(output_path).stem` instead. `mesh-bird.json` (the older, 2-days-stale, pure-duplicate file) was deleted after user confirmation -- nothing referenced it, and `entity-bird2.json`'s `"body"` part already resolved to `mesh-body.json`.
2. **Schema**: mesh JSON already had an unused `"name"` field (now finally trustworthy per task 1); added optional `"name"` to the part dict (inside an entity's `"parts"` array) and to entity JSON's own top level. All purely additive -- absent on every part/entity in every file that existed before this change, so display code falls back to `part.get("name") or part.get("id")` (and the entity/mesh equivalent) everywhere, no forced migration for old content beyond the hand-backfill in task 6.
3. **Part id creation → id (frozen) + name (editable)**, all 3 creation call sites in `entity_builder.py`: `_draw_parts_tab`'s "+ Add Part" (the text field is now the typed **name**; `state.new_part_id` renamed to `state.new_part_name`; the **id** is derived by running that same text through the existing `unique_part_id()` dedup, unchanged function, reused verbatim -- for a fresh, never-renamed part, id and name start identical, invisible until an actual rename happens); `_draw_scaffold_content`'s "Add Selected Parts" (the socket-derived candidate becomes the name, id still deduped the same way -- two parts sharing a display name after an id dedup suffix is an accepted, harmless outcome, since names aren't unique by design); `_add_part_for_converted_mesh` (id keeps deriving from `mesh_id_to_part_id(mesh_id)` unchanged, name prefers the mesh's own now-trustworthy `"name"` field via a new `read_mesh_name()` helper, falling back to the same derived string for an older mesh predating task 1's fix). `validate_new_part_id` renamed to `validate_new_part_name` and simplified to only reject an empty name -- a duplicate *name* is no longer an error (id collisions are impossible by construction once `unique_part_id` runs).
4. **New UI for actually renaming things**: `_draw_parts_tab`'s collapsing-header label switches to `part.get("name") or part_id`, with an editable "name" text field as the first field inside the header and a read-only `id: {part_id}` line below it for grep/debug visibility -- the header's own `##{part_id}` imgui-id suffix stays keyed on the immutable id, deliberately, so renaming a part never scrambles which header is open. `_draw_entity_info_window` gained an editable "Name" field (`state.entity_name`, new `BuilderState` field, defaults to `entity_id` when absent, loaded from/saved into the entity JSON's own `"name"`) alongside the existing read-only "Entity: {id}" line. `launcher.py`'s `_rename_asset()` was rewritten from the ground up: it used to rewrite the JSON's `"id"` field, rename the file, and migrate the manifest key (the exact "doesn't scan for references" hazard its own docstring flagged) -- it now only ever writes `"name"`, touching nothing else, with the file-rename/manifest-migration/collision-check code deleted entirely (names aren't unique, so there's nothing to collide with). Rename was previously entities-only in the launcher UI even though `_rename_asset()` itself was already category-generic -- widened to also cover `"meshes"` (materials deliberately left out, not asked for this round; extending later is a one-line UI-gate change, not a redesign, since the function itself needs no further changes). New `_current_display_name()` helper pre-fills the rename modal with the asset's actual current name, not its id.
5. **Defense-in-depth tripwire, not expected to ever fire**: confirmed `entity_template_editing.py`'s shared `draw_part_fields()` never touches `"id"` today, then added a guard anyway at both of its call sites -- `entity_builder.py`'s `_draw_parts_tab` and (found as an exact parallel exposure while implementing, not originally scoped, added for the same reason) `area_viewer.py`'s `_draw_template_section` -- so if a future change to that shared, cross-file editor ever started rewriting `id`, it gets restored and surfaced loudly (a toast) instead of silently corrupting a save. `area_viewer.py`'s own copy matters even more than `entity_builder.py`'s: its replacement matches parts by the *old* id, so a silently-changed id there would still land in the right list position but carry a value nothing else in that shared template actually points at.
6. **Migration for existing content** (real footprint: 2 entity files, 8 parts total) -- hand-edited, not scripted, given the tiny scale: added a top-level `"name"` (copy of the existing bare id) to `entity-example-staff.json` and `entity-bird2.json`, and a `"name"` (copy of the existing `"id"`) to each of their 8 total parts; re-ran `refresh_manifest()` once at the end. No changes needed to any animation clip file -- their `"parts"`/`"origins"` maps stay keyed by plain part-id strings by design; that's exactly the linkage this feature's immutable-id guarantee makes safe, not something to migrate.
7. **Explicitly deferred, stated not silently dropped**: mesh sockets (`attachTo.socket` targets) -- Blender-authored, no rename UI exists for them anywhere in this tool; materials' and animation clips' own ids -- same underlying hazard, `_rename_asset()` staying category-generic means extending to materials later is cheap, just not part of this round; combo/picker displays (mesh picker, attachTo-part picker, Animation Editor's part-assignment combo) still show ids, not names -- ids stay readable so this isn't required to satisfy "renaming doesn't break relations," left as a separable follow-up if wanted.
8. **Follow-up, per direct request**: "Have the entity list display the entities by their name, rather than ID." `launcher.py`'s Launcher window shares one rendering loop across its three asset-browser tabs (Meshes/Entities/Materials), all previously showing/sorting/filtering by raw id via a local `_filtered_sorted_keys()` closure. New module-level `filtered_sorted_entity_ids_by_name(entries, filter_text)` -- deliberately module-level rather than a `run()`-nested closure like its sibling, specifically so its real filter/sort logic is headlessly testable -- resolves each entity's current `_current_display_name()`, sorts by `(name.lower(), id)`, and matches the filter text against *both* name and id (someone might still search by the id shown in the row). Scoped to the Entities tab only, per the literal request; Meshes/Materials are untouched, still raw-id `_filtered_sorted_keys()`. The row label is `f"{display_name}  ({asset_id})"` (or just the id, unadorned, when name and id are identical -- true for every entity that predates this whole rename-safety feature), while the imgui widget id stays keyed on the immutable `asset_id` via the existing `##{category}-{asset_id}` suffix, so selection/open-state survives a rename exactly as it already did for parts.

## Step 15 — Animation Editor: "All Parts" Rigid-Group Transform ✅

Per direct request: "Add another option to the animation editor's keyframe transformer system that allows you to apply transformations to every mesh/part in the entity as one." Until now, a keyframe's position/rotation/scale fields were strictly per-part -- moving a whole multi-part entity (e.g. a bird jumping, a staff being swung) meant editing every assigned part's fields individually by the same amount, tedious and error-prone. **Design fork surfaced via `AskUserQuestion` before implementing** (per this session's own established practice of asking before deciding scope on a genuine architecture choice): a rigid-group delta that moves/rotates/scales every part together while each keeps its pose *relative to the others* (recommended and chosen), versus a "copy one part's transform to every other part" button (rejected -- would visually collapse a multi-part mesh's parts toward an identical pose, not what "as one" means for something with real spatial extent like a bird's wings vs. body).

1. **Pure delta math**, two new functions in `entity_builder.py`: `compute_group_transform_delta(old_position, new_position, old_rotation, new_rotation, old_scale, new_scale)` returns an additive position delta, an additive rotation delta, and a per-component scale *ratio* (guarding a near-zero old scale component against divide-by-zero -- dragging a scale field to exactly 0 is a legal, if unusual, widget state); `apply_rigid_group_delta(keyframe, part_ids, delta_position, delta_rotation, scale_ratio)` applies that delta/ratio to every listed part's own transform inside the keyframe, in place.
2. **New `BuilderState` fields**: `animation_editor_group_position`/`_rotation`/`_scale` (identity by default) and `animation_editor_group_kf_index` (a `-2` sentinel, so the very first draw always resets once before use). These three transform fields are a *running total since the control was last reset*, not a real transform read off any part -- each widget edit is applied to every part as the delta between the control's previous and new value, which is why raw absolute values wouldn't make sense to store per-keyframe or persist to disk; they're pure UI scratch state, reset to identity every time the selected keyframe changes (`animation_editor_group_kf_index != index`), since a stale running total from a different keyframe would be meaningless.
3. **New UI in `_draw_animation_editor_window`**: an "All Parts (apply to every part together)" collapsing header, placed above the per-part list, with its own position/rotation/scale `drag_float3` fields. Touching any of them: (a) auto-assigns every one of the entity's parts to the current keyframe that isn't already in it (identity transform first, per `assign_part_to_keyframe`) -- "every mesh/part in the entity" means literally every part, not just whichever ones happened to already be assigned; (b) computes the delta via task 1's pure function and applies it to every part via `apply_rigid_group_delta`; (c) updates the running-total state and calls `_sync_preview_definition`, same as every other field in this window.
4. **Explicitly not done**: no "undo"/"reset group control" button -- the control already implicitly resets on every keyframe switch, and this tool has no undo stack anywhere else either (see the module docstring), so a dedicated reset button here would be inconsistent with every other field in this file.

Verify: `python -m py_compile client/engine/entity_builder.py`. 9 new headless assertions in `run_entity_builder_test.py` (146 total, all passing): `compute_group_transform_delta` returns correct additive position/rotation deltas and a correct multiplicative scale ratio, reports a zero delta when old==new, and returns a `1.0` ratio (not a crash) for a near-zero old scale component; `apply_rigid_group_delta` shifts every listed part by the same additive position delta while each part keeps its own distinct position (proving it's a rigid group move, not an identical-position collapse), adds the same rotation delta on top of each part's own existing rotation, and multiplies each part's own scale by the same ratio component-wise. Live GPU verification drove the real `_draw_animation_editor_window` against the real `entity-example-staff` fixture (parts "shaft"/"charm"), forcing collapsing headers open and simulating a drag on each of the group control's three fields in turn (only "shaft" started assigned to the keyframe): confirmed the position drag correctly auto-assigned "charm" and moved both parts by the same `[10,0,0]` delta while preserving their different absolute positions; the rotation drag added `[0,0.5,0]` to both parts' existing rotation without touching position; the scale drag multiplied both parts' scale by `2.0` per axis; and switching to a second keyframe correctly reset the group control's running-total fields back to identity.

## Step 16 — Default Rest Pose When No Animation Is Selected, and Deselecting ✅

Per direct request: "When an entity is not set to an animation, set the part transitions [transforms] to their default state." **Scope clarified via `AskUserQuestion` before implementing** (a genuine two-part ambiguity): the fix applies to both the Entity Builder's own live preview and real gameplay `entity_renderer.py` (confirmed the latter was already correct -- see task 0), and the actual trigger is specifically the Animations tab's row-selection model, which had no way to *deselect* an animation once one was made active, and no explicit "nothing selected" default state either.

0. **Confirmed already correct, no change needed**: real gameplay `entity_renderer.py`'s `_draw_entity` already initializes `local_position`/`rotation`/`scale`/`origin` from the part's own `localOffset` *before* checking `action_animations`/`animation_id`, only overwriting them if `sampled` actually produced something -- a part with no matching action state and no `animation_id` already renders at its authored rest pose today. The gap was entirely in the Entity Builder's own preview path, below.
1. **Real gap, confirmed by reading the code, not theorized**: `_sync_preview_definition` wrote the scratch preview file from `state.parts` completely unchanged whenever no clip was open in the Animation Editor (`apply_keyframe_preview(state.parts, None, ...)` is a no-op by design). Since the preview entity is rendered by the real, production `EntityRenderer`, any part with its own real `animation_id` would immediately start playing continuously the moment an entity loaded in the builder -- even though nothing in the Animation Editor had ever been opened, and there was no way to see that part's plain authored rest pose at all.
2. **New pure `strip_live_animation_fields(parts)`**: returns a shallow copy of *parts* with every part's own `animation_id`/`action_animations` removed (localOffset untouched) -- same shallow-copy-and-strip technique `apply_keyframe_preview` already uses for a keyframe-assigned part, factored out since this case needs it applied to *every* part unconditionally, not just keyframe-assigned ones. `_sync_preview_definition` now branches on `state.animation_editor_clip is None`: no clip open uses this function (every part shows its default rest pose); a clip open keeps using `apply_keyframe_preview` exactly as before.
3. **New `_close_animation_editor(scene, state)`**, factored out of the Animation Editor window's own close-button handler (`if not keep_open:`) so the exact same deselect path -- clear `editing_animation_id`/`animation_editor_clip`/`animation_editor_path`/`animation_editor_selected_kf`, then `_sync_preview_definition` to snap back to default -- is reachable from more than one place.
4. **New ways to actually deselect, per direct request** ("make it possible to deselect a currently selected entity['s animation]"): in `_draw_animations_tab`'s table, clicking the *already-active* row now calls `_close_animation_editor` instead of redundantly reopening the same clip; a "Deselect Animation" button (shown only while one is active) does the same. The window's own close (X) button still works identically, now sharing the same helper.
5. **Real follow-up bug, found and fixed after a direct report**: "Creating another new animation for the bird entity does not add it to the animation list, and instead starts playing the flap-test animation. However it does not add flap-test to the animation editor." Not adding to the Animations tab's table on creation is expected/documented behavior (a brand-new clip has no part usage yet -- see `_draw_animations_tab`'s own docstring); the real bug was task 2's fix only checking `state.animation_editor_clip is None`, not whether a keyframe was actually selected/previewable. Opening a brand-new *empty* clip (`clip` is a real dict, just with zero keyframes -- `_open_animation_editor` leaves `animation_editor_selected_kf` at `-1` until a first keyframe exists to auto-select) still fell into the `apply_keyframe_preview` branch with `preview_keyframe=None`, a documented no-op -- so `entity-bird2`'s wing/leg parts' own real, continuous `animation_id` (`anim-transform-flap_test`) kept playing completely undisturbed, with nothing in the visibly-empty new editor explaining why the mesh was still moving. Fixed by keying the default-state branch off `preview_keyframe is None` instead of `clip is None` -- covers both "no clip open" and "clip open but nothing selected" with the one same rule, while leaving the documented "a keyframe *is* selected, but doesn't name every part" behavior (other parts' own animations keep playing alongside the one(s) being previewed) untouched.

Verify: `python -m py_compile client/engine/entity_builder.py`. 5 new headless assertions in `run_entity_builder_test.py` (151 total, all passing): `strip_live_animation_fields` removes `animation_id`/`action_animations`, leaves `localOffset` untouched, leaves a part with neither field alone, and never mutates the original list. Live GPU verification went beyond internal state: gave the real `entity-example-staff` fixture's "shaft" part (which has no `localOffset` of its own, so its authored default rest position is `[0,0,0]`) a real, continuous `animation_id` pointing at a clip that would move it to `[11,0,0]`, then read `EntityRenderer._draw_mesh_part`'s actual drawn world position at three points: on load, before the Animation Editor was ever opened -- `[0,0,0]`, confirming the animation did *not* auto-play; after explicitly opening that animation and selecting the keyframe posed at `[11,0,0]` -- correctly posed there; and after calling the real `_close_animation_editor` (the same path the row-reclick/button/window-close all now share) -- back to `[0,0,0]`, confirming deselecting genuinely returns the part to its default rest pose rather than leaving it mid-animation. Task 5's fix verified with its own live GPU script reproducing the exact report: opened the real `entity-bird2` fixture, replicated the "Create##new-animation" button's own code to create and open a brand-new empty clip (confirmed 0 keyframes, `selected_kf == -1`), then sampled `l_wing`'s actual drawn world matrix (`m00`, which flap_test's rotation would otherwise change continuously) at two points several frames apart -- identical both times, confirming flap_test no longer auto-plays. Full suite re-run afterward with zero regressions.

## Step 17 — Per-Part Transition Curve (Cubic-Bezier Easing) ✅

Per direct question ("What is the formula for this transition smoothness?"), it turned out there wasn't one -- `transform_clip.py`'s `_interpolate` was, and until now always had been, plain linear interpolation (`t = elapsed / span`, `value = lo + (hi - lo) * t`), no ease-in/ease-out curve of any kind. Direct follow-up request: "How hard would it be to implement into the animation editor the ability to edit the transition formula for each part in a keyframe" -- answered as an exploratory question (small/well-contained, one real design fork: a fixed named-easing set vs. a fully flexible curve). **User chose the flexible curve**, then, via `AskUserQuestion`, chose raw cubic-bezier control-point numbers **plus a live visual curve preview** over numbers alone.

1. **New pure math in `transform_clip.py`**: `DEFAULT_EASING = (0, 0, 1, 1)` (a straight line -- linear, unchanged old behavior); `resolve_easing(entry)` reads an entry's own `"easing"` field, defaulting to `DEFAULT_EASING` when absent/malformed (wrong length, wrong type) -- shared by the interpolation code and the new UI, so both always agree on what "no curve authored" means; `cubic_bezier_ease(t, x1, y1, x2, y2)` solves the parametric cubic-bezier curve `cubic-bezier(x1,y1,x2,y2)` (the same convention CSS/After Effects use) for `y` at a given `t` via a few Newton-Raphson iterations solving `x(u) = t` first (same reference algorithm WebKit's own `cubic-bezier()`/the CSS Easing Functions spec use) -- `t<=0`/`t>=1` short-circuit to exactly `0.0`/`1.0` rather than running Newton-Raphson at a boundary where its derivative can be degenerate.
2. **Wired into `_interpolate`**: computes `eased_t = cubic_bezier_ease(t, *resolve_easing(hi))` once per sample (`hi` being the *destination* keyframe of whichever segment `time_ms` falls in -- "ease into this pose" reads naturally as a property of the keyframe being eased into, keeping `"easing"` colocated with the pose it shapes) and uses `eased_t` in place of raw `t` for every field's lerp. The two hold-at-the-boundary branches already set `t = 0.0`, and `cubic_bezier_ease(0, ...)` is always exactly `0.0` regardless of curve, so easing has no effect outside a clip's actual time range. Because `sample_transform_clip`'s multi-part branch already merges a part's own `keyframe["parts"][part_id]` dict (via `**kf["parts"][part_id]`) into the flat per-part keyframe list `_interpolate` receives, an `"easing"` field placed inside that per-part dict flows through automatically -- no extra plumbing needed for the multi-part rig-clip schema specifically. Real gameplay's `entity_renderer.py`/`sample_part_pose`/`_update_playback_pose` all call `sample_transform_clip` unchanged, so every playback path (real gameplay, Timeline scrubbing, live preview) picks up easing for free.
3. **New UI in `_draw_animation_editor_window`**, per part per keyframe, right after the scale field: two `drag_float2` fields for the bezier control points `P1=(x1,y1)`/`P2=(x2,y2)`, writing `transform["easing"]`; `x1`/`x2` are clamped to `[0,1]` after each edit (a bezier curve is only a valid function of time otherwise, per CSS's own spec), `y1`/`y2` are deliberately left unclamped so an overshoot/"back"-style curve stays possible, matching CSS/AE. New `_draw_easing_curve_preview(x1,y1,x2,y2)`: hand-samples 24 points along the curve and draws them as a polyline via plain `ImDrawList.add_line` calls -- the same technique `client/engine/gizmo.py`'s own overlay already uses -- rather than imgui's built-in `plot_lines`, which needs a numpy `ndarray` and this codebase's own "nothing should import numpy directly" rule (`requirements.txt`) rules that out; the plotted y-range is padded beyond `[0,1]` so an overshoot curve stays visible instead of clipping flat against the box edges, and small circle markers show the two control-point handles.
4. **Real gap found and fixed while adding this, confirmed by reading the code, not theorized**: `duplicate_keyframe` used to hardcode a rebuilt dict containing exactly `position`/`rotation`/`scale` for each cloned part, which would have silently dropped a part's `"easing"` (or any other future per-part field) back to default the moment its keyframe was duplicated. Fixed to also carry over `"easing"` (as a fresh copy, preserving the existing "never share references back to the source" guarantee) when the source part has one.
5. **Docs kept in sync**: `docs/graphics/DATA_STRUCTURES.md`'s Transform Animation Clips schema table now documents the optional `"easing"` field and its default.

Verify: `python -m py_compile client/engine/transform_clip.py client/engine/entity_builder.py`. 17 new headless assertions in `run_entity_builder_test.py` (168 total, all passing): `resolve_easing` defaults correctly for absent/malformed/wrong-length input and round-trips a well-formed one; `cubic_bezier_ease` is exactly `0.0`/`1.0` at the boundaries regardless of curve, reduces to plain `t` for linear control points, is exactly symmetric (`0.5` at `t=0.5`) for the standard CSS ease-in-out curve, sits behind/ahead of linear at the midpoint for ease-in/ease-out curves respectively, and can overshoot past `1.0` for a "back"-style curve; `sample_transform_clip` actually applies an authored easing curve (not just raw linear `t`), stays exactly linear when none is authored, and is unaffected outside the clip's time range; `duplicate_keyframe` carries over an existing `"easing"` field as a real deep copy and doesn't invent one for a part that never had it. Live GPU verification drove the real `_draw_animation_editor_window`/`_update_playback_pose` against the real `entity-example-staff` fixture: forced collapsing headers open, simulated a drag on the P1 control point (a strong ease-in), confirmed it wrote the expected `[0.9, 0.05, 1.0, 1.0]` into the destination keyframe's own transform and that `_draw_easing_curve_preview` actually ran; then scrubbed the Timeline to the transition's exact midpoint and read `EntityRenderer._draw_mesh_part`'s real drawn world position -- `x≈1.53` with the ease-in curve vs. `x=5.0` with no easing authored at all, confirming the curve is genuinely wired through the entire real sampling/rendering pipeline, not just stored inert JSON. Root-caused one false-alarm crash during this verification to a bug in the *test script itself* (it selected keyframe 0 in the editor's UI but tried to read/target keyframe 1's own easing field -- a UI-shows-only-the-selected-keyframe's-fields mismatch), not the feature; fixed the script, not the product code.
